analysis.one_liner: Writes a narrow definition of federally protected waters permanently into law.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors, the bill was read twice and placed on the Senate calendar in January 2022, then died without a vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would take the definition of "waters of the United States" — the line that decides which streams, wetlands, and ponds fall under the Clean Water Act — out of the regulators' hands and write it permanently into federal law. The version it would lock in is the one from the regulation in effect on January 1, 2021, which covered fewer waters than earlier definitions. Smaller streams and wetlands outside that line would no longer need federal pollution permits, and only Congress could ever change the line again.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners and businesses that would otherwise need federal permits to fill, ditch, or discharge into smaller streams and wetlands — most visibly farmers, real estate developers, and energy and mining companies. The bill gives them a narrower, statute-locked definition that reduces federal permitting requirements and cannot be widened by a future administration without an act of Congress.

how_it_helps.text: The bill takes the definitions of "waters of the United States" from the regulation in effect on January 1, 2021 and enacts them into law, so they could no longer be rewritten by the EPA or the Army Corps of Engineers without Congress acting.
Enacting the definition by statute removes the regulatory flexibility that let each administration set the jurisdictional line, giving landowners and regulated businesses a fixed, predictable rule.

analysis.who_pays: People who rely on the smaller streams and wetlands that the narrower definition leaves outside federal protection — for drinking water sources, flood absorption, and pollution filtering — along with state agencies, which would shoulder more of the burden of policing water pollution with no federal backstop. Once the line is in statute, ordinary citizens could not restore protection to excluded waters without an act of Congress.
analysis.who_pays_short: Downstream communities and state water regulators

drawbacks.text: The definitions being enacted are the ones from the regulation in effect on January 1, 2021, which covered a narrower set of waters than prior definitions; waters outside that line — many streams and wetlands — would lose the federal Clean Water Act protections they had under broader readings, with consequences for downstream water quality.
Because the definition would sit in statute rather than regulation, only Congress could ever adjust it, eliminating the ability of expert agencies to update the jurisdictional line over time.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The genuine upside was regulatory certainty: landowners and businesses would know exactly which waters require a federal permit, without waiting on each new administration's rewrite. The cost was permanent: a narrower protection line locked into law, putting more streams and wetlands beyond federal oversight and leaving their fate with states of varying capacity and will. On balance, the bill traded durable public water protections for business certainty, and it never came close to a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate introduced the bill, read it twice, and set it on the calendar in January 2022, but never brought it up for a vote, and it expired when the 117th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Capito introduced the bill in the Senate on January 10, 2022.
No senator joined as a cosponsor; the cosponsor list stayed at zero.
The bill was read a second time and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders (Calendar No. 236) on January 18, 2022 — its last action.
No committee, floor debate, or vote followed; the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the narrower definition was never locked into statute and the jurisdictional line stayed open to the agencies' ongoing rulemaking; farmers, developers, and energy firms gained no statutory shield, and federal water protections remained in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal water rules stayed open to revision

for.name: Sen. Shelley Moore Capito
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and it was placed on the Senate calendar; it received no cosponsors and no further action.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the floor; after it was placed on the calendar on January 18, 2022, no vote or debate occurred for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican sponsored the bill, no senator of either party cosponsored it, and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The narrower statutory definition would exempt many farm ditches, wetlands, and ephemeral streams from federal Clean Water Act permitting, sparing farmers requirements and costs. Those same waters feed the drinking water and flood protection that downstream communities lose when pollution oversight narrows.

Locking in the narrower definition would shrink the wetlands and streams requiring federal permits before land is built on, cutting permitting costs and delays. The public bears the loss of wetlands that filter water and absorb floods.

A statute-locked narrow jurisdiction line would reduce the waters needing federal discharge or fill permits for pipelines, well pads, and mines, and would prevent any future administration from widening oversight by regulation. Discharges into newly excluded waters shift costs onto downstream water users.

With fewer waters under federal jurisdiction, states would inherit primary responsibility for policing pollution in excluded waters — more authority, but also more cost and work, and uneven protection depending on each state's rules.
